clue.text: Nudists need not fear this artful dodger

definitions.text: Nudists need not fear this artful dodger

parts.words: Nudists need not fear this artful dodger
parts.note: people wearing no clothes have no pockets, so a thief who lifts wallets from pockets has nothing to take from them

explanation.surface: A naturist colony has no reason to worry about a crafty thief.
explanation.walkthrough: The Artful Dodger is the young thief in Dickens's Oliver Twist; the joke is that nudists carry nothing worth stealing because they have nowhere to keep it.
explanation.definitionFit: A thief who steals from the clothing of passers-by, like the Artful Dodger, is a dip or cutpurse.

definitions.meaning: in Greek myth ... judged which goddess was fairest and gave the golden apple to Aphrodite

explanation.definitionFit: Paris is the French capital, and the Trojan prince of that name judged the beauty contest of the goddesses.

clue.text: The highest post to which a sailor may aspire?

definitions.text: The highest post to which a sailor may aspire?

parts.words: The highest post to which a sailor may aspire?
parts.note: the post is not a rank but the lookout platform at the top of the mast, the highest place a seaman can climb to

explanation.surface: A question about the top job open to a seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'post' suggests a rank or position in the navy; it is the lookout's perch at the masthead.
explanation.definitionFit: The lookout platform at the top of a ship's mast is the highest point a seaman can climb to.

clue.text: Drink suits the force to a T

parts.note: a posse is a body of men gathered to enforce the law
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drink fits the police force perfectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suits ... to a T' reads as an idiom for fitting exactly, but 'suits' only joins, and the T is added to POSSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A posset is a hot drink of milk curdled with ale or wine.

parts.note: wranglers are people who argue, and angry words exchanged in a quarrel are the same phrase as these word puzzles

explanation.surface: Language drills for Cambridge mathematics students.
explanation.walkthrough: A wrangler is also a Cambridge mathematics first-class graduate, which pulls towards academic exercises; here wranglers are quarrellers exchanging angry words.
explanation.definitionFit: Word puzzles of this kind share their name with the angry words exchanged by people quarrelling.

indicators.note: 'mysterious' suggests the word East is puzzled up into a strange new order

explanation.surface: Food from the exotic Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mysterious' asks you to rearrange EAST.
explanation.definitionFit: Grub and eats are both informal words for food.

indicators.note: a return comes back the other way, so the word for double is written backwards

parts.note: dual means double, twofold

explanation.surface: A sportsman is applauded for a double return of serve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns DUAL round to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol or glorify someone is to sing their praises; both are verbs.

clue.text: With this tree man attains dignity

definitions.text: With this tree man attains dignity

parts.words: With this tree man attains dignity
parts.note: put the name of a tree before the word man and you get a dignitary on a town council

explanation.surface: A man climbs a tree to gain respect.
explanation.walkthrough: The tree's name plus MAN makes ALDERMAN, a senior member of a borough or county council, so 'dignity' is the civic office.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree of the birch family, which with 'man' added names a senior civic dignitary.

clue.text: Wherein the traveller doesn't stop for meals

definitions.text: Wherein the traveller doesn't stop for meals

parts.words: Wherein the traveller doesn't stop for meals
parts.note: on a train the passenger eats while the train keeps moving, in a carriage set aside for meals

explanation.surface: A place where a traveller eats without breaking the journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't stop for meals' sounds like a traveller skipping food; in fact the journey does not stop while the passenger eats.
explanation.definitionFit: The railway carriage where passengers are served food while the train keeps running.

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says reclaim is only one possible order of these letters, so they are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Recovering something lost would be marvellous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' asks you to rearrange RECLAIM.
explanation.definitionFit: A marvel or wonder is an extraordinary event, like one attributed to a saint.

parts.note: a radical in mathematics is a root, and a play of 1959 by Arnold Wesker bears the plural of that word as its title

explanation.surface: A revolutionary piece of theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'radical' looks political, but it means a mathematical root (and comes from Latin radix, root); the play is Arnold Wesker's drama of rural Norfolk life.
explanation.definitionFit: Square roots and cube roots are called radicals, and Wesker's play has that word as its title.

clue.text: Those who are lose the lot .

definitions.text: Those who are lose the lot

parts.words: Those who are lose the lot
parts.note: at an auction, bidders beaten by a higher offer fail to win the lot under the hammer

explanation.surface: Some people lose everything they have.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lose the lot' suggests losing everything, but a lot is an item at an auction.
explanation.definitionFit: Bidders topped by a higher offer are beaten at auction and go home without the item.

clue.text: In which we find the sword of Damocles

definitions.text: In which we find the sword of Damocles

parts.words: In which we find the sword of Damocles
parts.note: the sword in the Greek legend hung over Damocles by a single hair, held in the air in an anxious state

explanation.surface: A reference book entry pointing to an old Greek legend.
explanation.walkthrough: The sword of Damocles was hung by a horsehair over his head; it is literally suspended, and the phrase stands for anxious uncertainty.
explanation.definitionFit: Anxious uncertainty about what will happen is the feeling of a threat hanging overhead, and the sword was literally hung.

parts.note: Juliet's speech in Romeo and Juliet continues 'all in black', picturing night as a dignified older woman in dark clothes

explanation.surface: A line quoted from Juliet's impatient speech awaiting nightfall.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is filled from Shakespeare: 'Come, civil night, Thou sober-suited matron, all in black' (Romeo and Juliet, Act 3 Scene 2).
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare pictures night as a staid, married older woman dressed soberly, which is what the missing word means.

clue.text: They carry their precious weight amidships

definitions.text: They carry their precious weight amidships

parts.words: They carry their precious weight amidships
parts.note: fast naval warships carry their heavy guns, torpedoes and engines in the middle of the hull

explanation.surface: Ships carrying a valuable cargo in the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'precious weight' suggests treasure; it is the armament of fast escort warships.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast naval escort warships named for their role in attacking torpedo boats.

indicators.note: 'No sir' tells you to have none of the letters of the word sir left in the word before it

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks if something should be done and gets a polite refusal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No sir' sounds like a reply, but 'No' removes S, I and R from DESIRED, leaving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A deed is something done, an act or action.

parts.note: the exam is a medical one, and those waiting for its outcome are hospital patients

explanation.surface: Students waiting for their exam results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'patiently' hides 'patient': the examination is a doctor's, not a school test.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor's identification of an illness from its symptoms is the outcome of a medical examination.

clue.text: Kipling's cat walking by his wild

definitions.text: Kipling's cat walking by his wild

parts.words: Kipling's cat walking by his wild
parts.note: Kipling's Just So story says the Cat walked by himself, waving his wild tail and walking by his wild self, ...

explanation.surface: A line about Kipling's independent cat from the Just So Stories.
explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's 'The Cat that Walked by Himself' the cat goes 'walking by his wild lone'; the gap takes the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's phrase 'by his wild lone' means all by himself, solitary.

clue.text: Not unreasonably it's for the chopper

parts.words: Not unreasonably it's for the chopper
parts.note: the first syllable is a piece of wood for an axeman to chop, and the whole is what someone uses to reason soundly

explanation.surface: It makes sense that something belongs to the woodcutter.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue splits the answer as LOG-IC: a log is what a chopper cuts, and the whole word is sound reasoning.
explanation.definitionFit: Sound reasoning is the opposite of the unreasonable, so a reasoned argument proceeds not unreasonably.

indicators.note: 'become' says the letters of the preceding words turn into something different, a new word

explanation.surface: An actor admits their performance has grown somewhat stiff and jerky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My acting's' gives the nine letters MYACTINGS for 'become' to rearrange. 'rather jerky' fits exercises done in sharp bursts.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical exercises of the gym are often vigorous and abrupt in movement.

clue.text: The little beast is allowed about always

indicators.note: 'about' puts the word for allowed around the word for always

parts.note: to let means to allow, past tense let
ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'

explanation.surface: A small animal is permitted to roam at all times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps LET round EVER. The answer is a young hare in its first year.
explanation.definitionFit: A young hare under a year old is a small animal, the beast of the clue.

clue.text: A worker joins the Sappers in a cave

parts.note: a worker is a worker ant, the sterile labourer of the colony
the Sappers is the nickname of the Royal Engineers, abbreviated RE

explanation.surface: A labourer teams up with army engineers working underground in a cavern.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sappers are the British Army's Royal Engineers (RE), who dig tunnels and trenches. The answer is a poetic word for a cave.
explanation.definitionFit: Antre is a literary word, used by Shakespeare in Othello, for a cavern.

parts.note: palmy days are prosperous times, but the clue also points to the fruit of a palm tree, which shares its name with a day on the calendar

explanation.surface: Someone recalls their prosperous golden days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'palmy days' means flourishing times, but here the palm is the tree whose fruit has the same name as a day of the month.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit of a desert palm tree is named the same as a day of the calendar, like the 4th of July.

parts.note: the title of an Eastern ruler, written backwards, spells rime, a coating of frost

explanation.surface: A performer's return to the stage is a flop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comeback' and 'frost' suggest a failed return (a frost is a flop); in fact the man's title backwards is RIME, a word for hoar frost.
explanation.definitionFit: An emir is a Muslim ruler or commander, the 'he' of the clue whose title read backwards is a frost.

parts.note: the escapologist Houdini famously freed himself from a restraining canvas jacket

explanation.surface: Clothing in the fashion of the escape artist.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the first word of straitjacket, the restraint Houdini escaped from.
explanation.definitionFit: A strait waistcoat or jacket is the restraining garment Houdini escaped from; strait means tight, confining.

parts.note: nuts or a nut means mad, crazy
Meg is a pet form of the name Margaret

explanation.surface: A crazy woman named Margaret owns some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that the answer is the seed of a tropical fruit rather than a fruit in the usual sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The spice is the kernel of the fruit of an East Indian tree, so it is fruit in a loose sense.

definitions.meaning: to sing a song in a carefree, rolling way
anglers ... by drawing a baited line behind a moving boat

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to sing merrily in rounds and to fish by trailing a line behind a boat.

clue.text: A tie here for the footballer

definitions.text: A tie here for the footballer

parts.words: A tie here for the footballer
parts.note: a tie suggests a drawn match, but here it is the cord a player ties to fasten his footwear

explanation.surface: A football match ends in a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'tie' in football is a drawn game or a cup fixture; here it is the string tied on a footballer's boot.
explanation.definitionFit: The cord that fastens a boot is the 'tie' a footballer does up before a match.

indicators.note: 'who reform' says the letters of those are formed again in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A reformer's moral nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'who reform' asks you to rearrange THOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: The distinctive spirit or moral nature of a person or group is their character.

parts.note: Keith Waterhouse's novel and play about Billy Fisher, a young man who invents fantastic tales, gives the hero this surname

explanation.surface: A man called Billy who tells tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'story-teller' is a euphemism for someone who tells fibs; Billy Fisher in Keith Waterhouse's 'Billy Liar' tells endless fantasies.
explanation.definitionFit: A teller of stories is a polite way of naming a fibber, one who tells untruths.

parts.note: a tall cylindrical silk hat shares its name with the flue that carries smoke away from a heater

explanation.surface: A recommendation for headgear to keep you warm.
explanation.walkthrough: The tall top hat is named after the flue on a stove; the clue suggests a hat chosen for warmth.
explanation.definitionFit: The tall silk top hat named after a heater's flue pipe, which takes the warm smoke away from a stove.

parts.note: a speaker who drops the letter H in words like 'ouse' leaves it unsaid, so when it is dropped nobody hears it

explanation.surface: Something that is never heard to fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropped' suggests something falling with a noise; dropping one's aitches is leaving the H sound off the start of words.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the letter H, the one dropped by Cockney speakers, so when dropped it cannot be heard.

indicators.note: 'maybe' says the word oils is one possible order of the letters, which can be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tank is suggested for keeping oils in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' tells you to rearrange OILS.
explanation.definitionFit: A tower or pit for keeping grain, fodder or fuel in is a store.

clue.text: Pointed objects of a businesslike come-down

definitions.meaning: small sharp nails with brass heads
getting down to ... means dropping the chatter and dealing with the facts

explanation.surface: Sharp items belonging to a no-nonsense descent.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass-headed nails are sharp; the idiom 'come down to brass tacks' means turning to the practical essentials.
